newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. to ask China to end poultry import curbs.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to ask China to end poultry import curbs.

text.p: The United States on Friday denied Chinese accusations of an outbreak of a disease in poultry in two U.S. states and said it sought talks with China to lift a ban on poultry imports from the areas.
"Newcastle disease broke out in pet birds only... All of the pet birds that were infected with the disease have been destroyed," a spokeswoman for the U.S. embassy in Beijing said by telephone.
She said she had no information on which U.S. states found pet birds with Newcastle disease or when the problems were discovered.
She said the United States was seeking to hold talks with Chinese quarantine officials to try to convince them to lift a ban on poultry from the U.S. states of Oklahoma and Missouri.
China announced the ban on Tuesday.
The official Xinhua news agency said five cases of the disease were discovered in Oklahoma and Missouri between July and September.
An official of China's State Bureau of Animal Plant and Quarantine, contacted by telephone, said the bureau was aware of the U.S. argument that the disease was found only in pet birds.
But the official said the United States had not formally requested talks with the bureau, the official said.

In October, China announced a ban on imports of poultry from 10 U.S. states because of fears it carried a virus called highly pathogenic avian influenza. China and the United States held talks on the issue and the ban did not go into effect.
China is the second-biggest market in the world, after Russia, for U.S. poultry products.
Some 330,000 tonnes of U.S. poultry products -- worth a total of $445 million -- were exported to China through Hong Kong last year, according to the U.S. Poultry and Egg Export Council.
Every day 700 tonnes of U.S. chicken feet are transported across the border from Hong Kong into China, the council said.
Beijing and Washington are also at odds over textile imports, and that dispute has threatened to spill over into the farm sector.
China had threatened to ban effective last Tuesday some U.S. farm goods -- as well as textiles and alcoholic drinks -- in retaliation for U.S. penalties on textiles purchased from China.
Beijing however announced this week it was delaying implementing for one month those curbs because the two sides were planning further talks on the issue.
